events.title: SOAP 1.1 published
events.summary: The [W3C] published SOAP 1.1 as a Note on May 8, 2000 — an [XML] envelope format for remote procedure calls over [HTTP].
events.about: SOAP wrapped method calls in [XML] envelopes with headers and bodies — the backbone of early .NET ASMX services, [Java] JAX-WS, and enterprise B2B integrations. WSDL described endpoints; the WS-* stack added security and reliability. [Teams] used it when schemas, tooling, and corporate standards mattered more than [JSON] simplicity.

narrative.whyChosen: SOAP standardized [XML] web services for a decade of enterprise and government integrations.
narrative.whyImportant: It let [Java] and .NET systems interoperate through contract-first WSDL tooling.
narrative.problemSolved: Ad-hoc [XML] RPC needed a common envelope, encoding rules, and [HTTP] binding for multi-vendor systems.

events.title: ILOVEYOU worm infects millions of PCs
events.summary: The ILOVEYOU [worm] spread globally on May 4, 2000 — a Visual Basic Script attachment named LOVE-LETTER-FOR-YOU that overwrote files and mailed itself via Outlook.
events.about: ILOVEYOU caused an estimated $10 billion in damage — parliaments and corporations shut down email systems. It followed Melissa's playbook with nastier payloads and proved users would open romantic subject lines without hesitation. [Microsoft] later hardened default script execution, but social engineering remained undefeated.

narrative.whyChosen: ILOVEYOU was the most destructive email [worm] of the early internet era.
narrative.whyImportant: It made email attachment policies and user training non-optional for enterprises.
narrative.problemSolved: Nothing initially — it exploited trust and default Windows scripting with devastating speed.
